title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
text:
Introduction
This book follows one experiment: growing a brain in a simulation, one piece at a time, in roughly the order in which brains are thought to have evolved.
Each stage adds a small circuit to the brain of the previous stage and changes the world so that the new circuit has something to be good for. Evolution then gets a number of generations to put the circuit to use. A page of this book is the report of one stage: what was added and why, the biology it is modelled on, and what happened.
The concept of explaining cognition in steps following evolution is heavily inspired by the book A Brief History Of Intelligence by Max Bennett. However, the individual stages do not match one-to-one with the experiments mentioned in the book, and (while I do recommend it) it is not necessary to have read Bennett’s work to be able to follow along.
Disclaimer: this work is not guaranteed to be scientifically accurate and match exactly with real brains. It is a unique blend between staying close to nature, but also just “going for it” and building up to something advanced based on what works, not restricted by having every choice requiring a citation. I personally think that, while not scientific enough to be applicable to medicine, and not optimized enough to replace machine learning algorithms, understanding these experiments builds intuition about intelligence that could seriously prove useful in either domain.

title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
text:
The animals and their world
The animals live on a grid. Each has a stomach that empties a little every tick (one tick is about a second of behaviour) and faster when it moves. An animal whose stomach is empty dies.
Food grows on bushes. A bush carries a few berries, and once the last one is eaten it stays empty for a long time, longer than a full stomach lasts, and then has all its berries back at once. Waiting beside an empty bush costs more than the bush will give, so an animal has to keep moving. At the start of a life most bushes are empty and somewhere along their regrowth, as in a world that has been grazed for a while. Through a life, food therefore comes at a steady rate: a small share of the bushes carries berries at any moment. A bite costs a little energy.
The objects, their names and their pictures come from the game One Hour One Life. The simulation uses a small slice of the game’s rules at each stage and a larger one as the brain grows.
An animal senses the world through a few coarse “eyes”: a handful of directions, in each of which it sees whether something is there, how near it is, and what it looks like. What something looks like is a short list of numbers, its appearance. It can step forward, turn left or right, and grasp what is in front of it.

title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
text:
The brain
The brain is a network of model neurons. A neuron has an activity between 0 and 1 and passes it on through synapses, each with a strength. A neuron is either excitatory (it raises the activity of the neurons it reaches) or inhibitory (it lowers it), never both. Neurons are grouped into regions, and a projection is the set of synapses from one region to another.
Some projections are evolved: which synapses exist and how strong they are is inherited, with mutations, and shaped by selection. Others are hard-wired: they are designed, and evolution can only make the whole projection stronger or weaker. A hard-wired projection gives a group of neurons a fixed meaning, such as “this hurts”, that later stages can build on.

title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
text:
How evolution runs
A population is a set of genomes, each describing evolved synapse strengths and neuromodulator properties. Each genome lives as multiple siblings in a shared world. The genomes that did best have children, each from two parents, with a few mutations. That is one generation.
Fitness is what selection rewards. Here it is the well-fed lifetime: how long the animal lived, counted from its first meal, with each tick weighted by how full its stomach was. An animal that never eats scores zero.
Evolved genomes are carried over to following stages, instead of starting from scratch any time a new module is added.

title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
text:
How a stage is judged
One life is mostly luck, and one evolution run can end almost anywhere. So every stage is run three times with different random seeds, and every result is given as a mean with its standard error over those seeds.
Each stage has a main run, with the new circuit, and a control: the brain of the previous stage in the same new world, starting from the same population. The new circuit is then the only difference between them.
A stage succeeds when two things hold:

The circuit is used. The final population is put back in its world with the new neurons silenced. If the animals do clearly worse without them, in every seed, they were using them. This is called a lesion test.
Main is not worse than control. It does not have to be better. The point of some stages is a circuit that later stages can build on.

A circuit that is not used is left out of the brain, and the page says so.

title: Evolving a brain, stage by stage
section: How to read a stage page
text:
How to read a stage page
Every page has the same parts: the idea and its biology, the circuit as a diagram, the results, and the list of runs behind them, with a link to a dashboard that replays the last generation of a run. Where it helps, a page zooms in on one animal over a few dozen ticks, so that you can watch the circuit work.
The numbers, graphs and diagrams are drawn from data files that are written when a stage is run. Only the text is written by hand.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 1: steering
This page says where the book is going. Only the first chapter is written. Everything after it is a plan, and the plan changes as the experiments come in: stages have already been moved, merged and left out, and that will happen again.
The order follows the five breakthroughs of A Brief History of Intelligence. Each is one chapter, each belongs to a group of animals, and each builds on the brain of the chapter before it.
The brain of a small worm. It turns what it sees into movement (Steering), sorts the world into good and bad (Valence: good and bad), stops reacting to what is always there (Habituation: getting used to what is always there), learns in one life which new foods hurt (Association: learning what is bad), looks after hunger and cold (Drives: hunger and cold), and stays in a state for a while after a meal or a poison bite (Affect: states that last).
This animal learns one thing: what to stay away from. It cannot learn what is worth going to, and it cannot learn what to do.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 2: reinforcing
The brain of an early fish. The first vertebrates hunted in open water, and nearly all the parts of the vertebrate brain were already there. This chapter adds them in the following order.

Sharper eyes. The animal sees in more directions and further, in a world where good and poison bushes stand side by side again. The map of the visual field that vertebrates have, the tectum, is left out for now: it answers to things that move, and nothing in this world does. It returns when something can choose where to turn.
The pallium. The first region whose wiring is not inherited at all. It spreads the look of a thing out over many cells, so that things that look alike can still be told apart. In chapter 1, what the animal learned about one food spread to the foods that resembled it.
Dopamine. A cell that fires when things turn out better than expected, and falls silent when they turn out worse. With it the animal learns what predicts food, and what predicts the thing that predicts food. It also learns to like, which chapter 1 could not do.
Hands. Until here the animal eats what it grasps. Now it can pick something up, hold it and eat it later, so that there is something to choose between.
The basal ganglia. The same dopamine signal teaches which action to take. This is learning by trial and error, as in a rat that learns to press a lever.
Curiosity. New things become a little rewarding in themselves, so that the animal tries what it does not know yet.

Parked until these work: a map of places and the routes between them (the hippocampus), precise timing (the cerebellum), and modulators that set how fast the animal learns when its world is steady or changing.
Two things change in how the stages are done. The circuits are designed and tested before any evolution, and evolution then tunes them, in fewer generations than in chapter 1. And the learning stages get lab experiments: one animal in a scripted situation, as in an animal lab, to see whether it learns the way real animals do.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 3: simulating
The brain of an early mammal, and its new part, the neocortex. The cortex learns to predict what the animal will sense next. Once it can do that, it can be run without the world: the animal stops at a choice, plays out each option, and picks the one that ends best.
The planned stages: a cortex that predicts, trying actions in the head at a choice point, replaying experience during rest and sleep, holding a goal through distractions, and remembering a single event.
The tests are the classic ones from the rat lab. An animal that explored a maze without reward goes straight to food that appears there later. An animal whose path is blocked takes a detour. An animal that has had enough of one food stops working for it at once.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 4: mentalizing
The brain of a primate, living in a group in which the others matter. The brain first gets a model of itself: what it knows, and how sure it is. Applied to another animal, the same model says what that animal wants and what it has seen.
The planned stages: knowing when it does not know, reading the goals of others, learning a skill by watching, and preparing for a need it does not feel yet, such as storing food before the winter.

title: Roadmap
text:
Chapter 5: speaking
The human step. Calls with a fixed meaning come first, then signals whose meaning is agreed on within a group, then naming what two animals are both looking at. The aim at the end is knowledge that no single life could find again and that still grows from one generation to the next.
This chapter is the least certain, both in what is known about evolution and in whether a small grid world can carry it.

title: Roadmap
text:
The world grows too
A brain can only be tested on what its world asks of it, so the world grows with the brain. It takes more and more of the rules of One Hour One Life: tools, fire and cooking, and chains of steps that are too long to find by accident. Animals that move by themselves come in as prey and as predators.
For the last two chapters, the way lives are run has to change as well. A generation now starts and ends together. Animals that watch, imitate and teach each other need parents, children and lives that overlap.

title: Steering
text:
The world: berries and onions
The first animal has no memory, no hunger and no idea of good or bad. It can do one thing: turn what it sees into movement. This stage evolves a brain that does that, from random wiring, until the animal finds food and eats it.
Everything after this stage is added to this brain.
The world holds four kinds of berry bush and wild onions. All of it is food and nothing is dangerous. An animal that stands still starves, and so does one that walks without getting anywhere, because moving costs energy. The only way to live is to get to a bush that carries berries, bite, and go on to the next one.
The animal eats what it grasps. Picking something up and carrying it comes much later.

title: Steering
text:
The biology: steering
The oldest animals with a front and a back were small worms, and what set them apart from jellyfish and sponges was that they could go somewhere. A body with a front end, sense organs on it, and a clump of neurons behind them can do something a net of nerves spread through the body cannot: turn towards what is good and away from what is bad. In A Brief History of Intelligence this is the first of the breakthroughs, steering.
The circuit for it is small. In the worm C. elegans, with 302 neurons, sensory neurons connect to a few layers of interneurons, and those to the motor neurons, with some sensory neurons wired to motor neurons directly. A direct connection is a reflex. The interneurons in between let several senses be weighed against each other before the muscles move.

title: Steering
text:
The circuit

A ganglion of sixteen excitatory and eight inhibitory interneurons. The eyes connect to it, its neurons connect to each other, and it connects to the motor neurons.
Reflex arcs: direct connections from the eyes to the motor neurons.

Every synapse in this brain is evolved: which ones exist, and how strong they are. Nothing is designed and nothing changes during a life.
The brain sees the outside world only. It does not feel its stomach, and it does not notice whether a bite gave it anything. Those senses enter the brain in later stages, through cells made for them.

title: Steering
text:
Watching it work
One animal from the last generation, walking up to a bush and eating. The rows below the picture are the neurons of the ganglion; there is nothing in them to read, and that is the point. No neuron here stands for anything. The behaviour is spread over all of them, wherever evolution happened to put it.

title: Steering
text:
Results
The curve has two parts. The brain first evolves from random wiring in short lives, because at the start nearly every animal dies young and longer lives would only cost computing time. Then the population is given lives four times as long, and the curve jumps: the same animals can now collect four times as much well-fed lifetime. In a short life an animal that ate once and then stood still could reach the end. In a long life it cannot, and over the generations that follow the standing still is selected away. Every later stage has these long lives.






This stage has no control: there is no earlier brain to compare it with. The lesions show the only thing they can here, that the animal depends on its ganglion. The direct reflex arcs alone are far from enough.









NoteWhat did not work: all the food at once





In earlier runs every bush was full when the animals were born. The animals filled their stomachs within the first tenth of their life and kept eating, the bushes were stripped by the middle of it, and since a bush takes long to regrow, most animals then starved together. Whatever an animal might have done better later in life could not show, and holding back could not pay: whoever waited found nothing left.
Starting most bushes empty, each at a random point of its regrowth, turned that stock into a steady flow. The share of bushes carrying berries now stays about the same from the first tenth of a life to its end, and so does the average stomach. The animals still bite when their stomach is full; nothing in this brain can feel the stomach yet.

title: Valence: good and bad
text:
The world: two kinds of berry are poison
The animal of the previous stage steers by reflex. What it sees is wired, through a small ganglion, straight to its motor neurons. It has no way of knowing what happened after it bit something.
This stage gives it that. It adds a handful of neurons that stand for this is good and this is bad, and puts food in the world that is bad to eat.
There are now six kinds of berry bush instead of four. They look alike, in the way that different berries look alike: each kind has the shape of a bush and its own colour.
Four kinds are food. Two are poison, and always the same two. Eating a poison berry empties the stomach by about as much as a good berry fills it, and it hurts for a moment.
Because the same two kinds are poison in every life, nothing has to be learned during a life. Which colours to avoid can be inherited. Learning it within a life is the subject of a later stage.

title: Valence: good and bad
text:
The biology: valence
In small animals, most sensory neurons fall into two classes. Some respond to things worth approaching, such as the smell of food. Others respond to things worth avoiding, such as a harmful chemical or a hard touch on the nose. The two classes converge onto a few interneurons that bias the animal towards carrying on or turning away.
Valence is the name for this sorting of the world into good and bad. In the worm C. elegans, a much-studied animal with 302 neurons, harmful stimuli do two things at once: they trigger a turn, and they stop the pumping of the throat with which the worm feeds. Max Bennett argues that this sorting is what the first brains were for.
The worm is only a stand-in. The animal that this chapter is about, the common ancestor of animals with a left and a right side, left no nervous system to look at.

title: Valence: good and bad
text:
The circuit
Five new groups of neurons, each with a meaning that is fixed by its wiring:

valence_app, the appetitive cells: active when something is good. The sense of taste is hard-wired to them, and reaches the brain nowhere else.
valence_av, the aversive cells: active when something is bad. Pain is hard-wired to them, and reaches the brain nowhere else.
grasp, a motor programme: when it fires, the animal bites what is in front of it.
no_touch, a gate: an inhibitory cell that is active whenever nothing is directly ahead, and holds grasp shut.
no_feed: an inhibitory pair driven by the aversive cells, which blocks the bite.

Taste and pain are unconditioned signals: they mean good and bad without any experience. But they arrive only after the bite. To act in time, the value cells also get input from the eyes, and that input is evolved. Over generations, the look of a poison berry comes to excite the aversive cells before anything has been eaten.
Value does not move the animal by itself. The appetitive cells excite grasp, but grasp can only fire when no_touch is silent, that is, when something is within reach. Releasing an action by switching off its inhibition is called disinhibition, and it is a common arrangement in real nervous systems. Here it makes a value turn into the right action for the situation: bite when the good thing is in front of the mouth, and not before.
The aversive cells do what the worm does. They drive the motor neurons for turning, and through no_feed they shut down biting.



Hover over a box or an arrow for details. The dark arrows are the designed wiring described above. The grey ones were left to evolution.

title: Valence: good and bad
text:
Watching it work
Below is one animal from the last generation, around the moment it bites a poison berry.
Step through it one tick at a time. At the bite, nothing in the brain has changed yet: the pain arrives with the next tick. Then the pain sense is on, both aversive cells fire, no_feed switches on and grasp falls silent. The animal turns away. A few ticks later the pain has faded and it is eating again.



Nothing was learned here. The animal will react in the same way the next time. What stops it from biting poison often is the evolved input from the eyes, which acts before the bite.

title: Valence: good and bad
text:
Results

Main against control
The control is the brain of the previous stage in this world. It cannot feel pain or taste at all, so it can only avoid poison if evolution happens to wire the look of the poison berries to turning away.



The three main curves do not rise at the same moment. Evolution has to find the wiring from the look of the two poison kinds to the aversive cells, and when it finds it is a matter of luck. One seed found it within a few generations. The two others were still climbing when the planned generations were over and were given as many again.



In principle the control can end up where main does. The poison looks the same in every generation, so pain tells the animal nothing that the colour of the bush does not, and a brain without pain can evolve “this colour, turn away” in its reflex wiring. So the gap between the curves does not say what pain is worth. It says how much easier the value cells make the solution to find: main has a ready path from the look of a berry to a cell that turns the animal away and stops the bite, and it starts out with a reaction to the pain itself.
Whether a control finds the solution within the generations it is given is a matter of luck. In earlier runs, with short lives and many more generations, two of three controls did, late and suddenly, after dozens of generations without progress. If a control’s curve above stays flat, that control had not found it yet.
The three rows measure the same thing with less and less noise. The first is taken from the generations as they ran. The second gives every final population the same eight worlds. In the third, main and control animals live together and compete for the same bushes, so a difference cannot come from one population having had an easier world.


Is the circuit used?



Read this chart region by region. A short bar means the animals depended on that region. A bar near 100 means they did as well without it, and three dots far apart mean the seeds disagree.
The two halves of the circuit are not used equally. The aversive side, valence_av and no_feed, is what the animals depend on. The appetitive side, valence_app and grasp, matters much less: the reflexes of the previous stage already bring the animal to food and make it bite.






NoteWhat did not work: appetite on a full stomach





In the first runs of this stage the animals were born with a full stomach, and the appetitive side was not used at all: silencing valence_app, no_touch or grasp left them as well off as before. A full stomach lasted for most of a life, so there was little to gain from eating well. Born a quarter full, the animals depend on the appetitive side a little, as the chart shows.
One fault remains. The appetitive side makes the animal bite whenever food is in reach, hungry or not, and a large share of all bites lands on a stomach that is nearly full. Nothing in this brain can sense the stomach. That comes with a later stage, which adds a cell for hunger.

title: Habituation: getting used to what is always there
text:
The world: a bush that never has berries
The animals of the previous stage know good from bad, and they respond to a look in the same way every time they see it. To them a bush that has been emptied still looks enough like food to bite at, and the look does not change however often the bite gives nothing. So an animal can stand in front of an empty bush for a long time, biting. What is missing is simple to say: an animal should stop responding to something that stays the same and keeps giving nothing.
This stage changes one thing, in the eyes.
The world of the previous stage gets one more kind of bush, a dud. It looks like a berry bush and never carries a berry. Its colour is drawn anew for every life, so nothing an ancestor knew about colours can tell an animal to leave it alone. In some lives the dud happens to have a colour the animal finds attractive, and then an animal that responds to a look in the same way every time will stand at it and bite for as long as it lives.
There are as many bushes with berries as before; the duds come on top.
crumbs: 3  Habituation: getting used to what is always there

title: Habituation: getting used to what is always there
text:
NoteWhat did not work: making the food unfamiliar





Without the dud, in the world of the previous stage, the change of this stage was used only a little. The long lives had already selected most of the standing still away, and evolution can learn the look of an empty bush of every kind it has always known.
Giving the good berries a new colour in every life did not change that. The animals with adapting eyes did slightly worse than those without. What makes adaptation worth having is something that looks like food and gives nothing, whatever colour it has.
crumbs: 3  Habituation: getting used to what is always there

title: Habituation: getting used to what is always there
text:
The biology: adaptation and habituation
Step into a room with a strong smell and after a few minutes it is gone. The smell is still there; the receptors have stopped reporting it. Sensory neurons respond to change: to what differs from the recent past. A steady input is the background, and the background carries no news. This is sensory adaptation.
Habituation is the same thing seen in behaviour. A snail that is touched pulls in its horns. Touch it again and again and it stops bothering. It is the simplest kind of learning there is, older than learning by association, and found in every animal that has been tested, including ones with a few hundred neurons.
crumbs: 3  Habituation: getting used to what is always there

title: Habituation: getting used to what is always there
text:
The circuit
No new cells. Each of the eyes’ look inputs now keeps a slow average of what it has been seeing, over roughly the last fifty ticks, and passes on the difference between what it sees now and that average.
Two things follow, both for the whole brain, because every neuron downstream of the eyes now gets the adapted look:

What stays in view fades. An animal that stands in front of a bush sees its look sink into the average. The appetitive cells, driven by that look, fall silent, and with them the urge to bite. The animal moves on.
What is unusual stands out. All berry bushes look alike in most respects, and that shared part is nearly always in view, so it is nearly always in the average. What passes through is the part that differs: the colour of this bush. Nothing uses this yet. It becomes important in the next stage, where the animal learns from a single bite which colour is bad.
crumbs: 3  Habituation: getting used to what is always there

title: Habituation: getting used to what is always there
text:
Watching it work
One animal from the last generation, at a dud. The two rows marked vis+0 are two of the look inputs of the eye that points straight ahead, the two that respond most strongly to this dud.
The animal walks up and bites. Step through the ticks and watch the two look inputs: the dud does not change, and yet what the eye reports sinks a little with every tick, because the eye is getting used to it. The appetitive cells and grasp do not fade as smoothly. They hold for a while and then drop out, and the biting stops.
Then the animal turns away, and the look inputs go below zero. Nothing is in front of the eye now, but the eye is still used to the dud, and what it reports is the difference: less of that look than usual.



Not every visit to a dud goes like this. Most are over within a few ticks, and some last far longer.
crumbs: 3  Habituation: getting used to what is always there

title: Habituation: getting used to what is always there
text:
Results
The control is the brain of the previous stage, with eyes that do not adapt, in the same world. Its fitness swings from one generation to the next: every generation draws a new colour for the dud, and how well these animals do depends on whether they happen to like it.
The first generations of main are a step back. Every synapse the animals inherit was shaped by eyes that reported the whole look, and now reports only the difference. The population has to re-tune before the change can pay.






The test in which main and control animals share a world is left out for this stage. In that test both halves run on the same brain, and here the difference is the brain’s inputs: the control animals would be given adapting eyes that none of their synapses were tuned to.

How a life is spent





Is it used?
There is no group of neurons to silence here, since the change is in how the inputs work. The matching test is to switch the adaptation off in the final population and let the same animals live in the same worlds again.



The lesions of the regions are shown for completeness.

title: Association: learning what is bad
text:
The world: nothing is familiar
Until now everything the animal knows was put there by evolution. That works for poison that looks the same in every generation. It cannot work for food that is new.
This stage adds the simplest kind of learning from experience: after a bite that hurts, the look of what was bitten comes to mean bad.
There are four kinds of berry bush, and all four are new in every life. Each life draws a new colour for every kind, and draws which two of the four are poison. Nothing an ancestor learned about colours is worth inheriting.
The bushes still look like berry bushes. A new kind differs from the others in its colour, not in its shape, the way a new berry is recognisable as a berry.
A poison berry costs about what a good berry gives, and it hurts for one tick. Half of all bushes are poison, so an animal that cannot learn pays that price on every second bush it tries, for as long as it lives. Leaving everything unknown alone is not an option either: there is nothing else to eat.
There are no duds in this world. What the eyes learned to do in the previous stage stays, and this stage builds on it.
crumbs: 4  Association: learning what is bad

title: Association: learning what is bad
text:
NoteWhat did not work: a world where learning was hardly worth it





The first versions of this world kept a familiar, safe kind of berry as half of all bushes, so that an animal that learned nothing would still get by. It got by very well: it ate about eleven good berries for every poison one. A perfect learner would have gained less than a tenth of its food. With so little to win, a lesson had to be nearly free of side effects to pay at all, and evolution switched learning off whenever it was not.
Removing the familiar food turned this around. In the world above, a perfect learner would save about a quarter of what it eats.
crumbs: 4  Association: learning what is bad

title: Association: learning what is bad
text:
The biology: learning by association
A sea slug that is shocked after a touch learns to pull back from the touch. A rat that gets sick after a new food avoids that food afterwards. This is associative learning: something neutral (the touch, the taste) comes to predict something that already matters (the shock, the sickness), and the animal starts to respond to the first as it would to the second.
The synapse-level picture, worked out in the sea slug Aplysia and the fruit fly, has three parts. A sensory neuron that was just active leaves a short-lived trace at its synapses. A teaching signal, released when something bad happens, reaches many synapses at once. Only the synapses that carry a fresh trace are strengthened. Pain says something bad happened; the trace says and this is what was there.
crumbs: 4  Association: learning what is bad

title: Association: learning what is bad
text:
The circuit
One new cell and one change to existing synapses:

us_pain, the teacher: driven by pain alone. When it fires, it broadcasts a teaching signal.
The synapses from the eyes’ look inputs onto the aversive cells valence_av, which evolution shaped in the previous stage, can now also change during a life. A synapse grows when its input was just active and the teacher fires.

The aversive cells already turn the animal away and block the bite. So nothing else has to change: once the look of a berry excites them, the animal treats that berry as it treats the poison it was born knowing.




What exactly gets blamed
A bite hurts, and something has to take the blame. Getting this right turned out to be most of the work of this stage, and three things were needed, the first of which the animals already bring with them.
The lesson is about what sets the food apart. All berry bushes look alike in most respects. If pain strengthened the synapses of the whole look, one bad red berry would make the animal wary of every berry. This is where the adapting eyes of the previous stage pay a second time: they pass on the difference between the look right now and what they usually see. What all bushes share cancels out before it reaches a synapse. What is left to take the blame is the colour.
The pain is brief. While pain faded over several ticks, the teacher was still firing after the animal had turned away, and by then its eyes were on the next bush. The animal learned to distrust the neighbour of the poison as much as the poison.
Every learned synapse exists. The look synapses were sparse, as evolution had left them, and a synapse that is not there cannot learn. In this stage all of them are present, the new ones starting at zero.






NoteWhat did not work: unlearning by tasting again





An earlier design had a second cell that lowered the aversion whenever something the animal distrusted turned out to taste fine. It worked when meals were fed to the brain in a test. In a living animal it never fired: aversion blocks the bite, so food that is distrusted is never tasted again, and the mistake cannot be found out.
This is why the lesson has to land on the right food in the first place.
crumbs: 4  Association: learning what is bad

title: Association: learning what is bad
text:
Watching it work
One animal from the last generation, at two moments of its life.
First, its first bite of a kind of berry that is poison in this life. Before the bite the aversive cells are silent and grasp fires. One tick after the bite the pain arrives, the teacher us_pain fires, and the aversive cells and no_feed switch on by reflex, as in the previous stage. What cannot be seen is the change the teacher leaves behind in the synapses.



Later in the same life the animal comes up to a bush of the same kind. Nothing hurts now, and yet the aversive cells fire and no_feed holds the bite back. The animal moves on. It learned this; no ancestor could have told it.

title: Association: learning what is bad
text:
Results

Main against control
The control is the brain of the previous stage in this world, adapting eyes included: it feels pain and turns away from it, but it cannot change. It pays for every poison bush it tries, every time.








Is the circuit used?



no_plasticity freezes every synapse at its inherited strength, and us_pain silences the teacher. If the animals do clearly worse without either, they depend on what they learn during their life.


How a life is spent
Few animals live out the long life this world offers: half of what they try is poison, and nothing tells an animal that it is getting hungry.

title: Drives: hunger and cold
text:
The world: cold, with warm places
Until now the brain has only looked outward. It sees, it tastes and it feels pain, but it has no idea how full its stomach is or how warm its body is. An animal that cannot feel its own state can do only one thing at a time, all the time: these animals forage whether they are starving or stuffed.
This stage gives the body a second need, warmth, and gives the brain two cells that report on the body. With two needs there is, for the first time, something to decide: which one to look after now.
The world of the previous stage becomes cold. A cold body burns its food faster, so an animal that stays cold starves sooner. Scattered through the world are a few hot springs, each warming the ground around it. An animal warms up slowly when it is near one and cools down slowly when it leaves.
The animal cannot see where it is warm. It feels the temperature of its own skin and nothing more.
The food is as before: four kinds of berry bush, new in every life, half of them poison.

title: Drives: hunger and cold
text:
The biology: drives
A drive is a signal from the body about something it needs: food, water, warmth, sleep. In vertebrates these signals are gathered in the hypothalamus, where small groups of neurons read the blood and the body and fire when a need is not met. They do not move a muscle themselves. They change what the rest of the brain does: which behaviour is switched on, and which is held back.
The way the animals here find warmth is older still. A bacterium or a worm that is in a bad place does not know where the good place is. It moves, and when things are good it stops moving. This is kinesis: no map and no sense of direction, only a rule about when to keep going. It is enough to end up, most of the time, where it is good.

title: Drives: hunger and cold
text:
The circuit
Four new cells.

cold fires while the skin is cold.
warm_seek is driven by cold and pushes the animal forward: keep moving while it is cold.
rest is an inhibitory cell that fires while the skin is warm and holds the forward step back: stay where it is warm.
hungry is an inhibitory cell that fires when the stomach is less than about two thirds full. It shuts both warm_seek and rest. A hungry animal forgets about warmth and forages as it did before; a fed animal looks after its temperature.

All of these connections are designed, and evolution may tune their strength. One set is left to evolution entirely: synapses from hungry onto the cells that feed (the grasp programme, the cell that blocks the bite, the appetitive cells and the ganglion). They start at zero. If it pays to bite less on a full stomach, this is where evolution can build it.

title: Drives: hunger and cold
text:
Results

Main against control
The control is the brain of the previous stage in this cold world. It gets cold and pays for it, and can do nothing about it, because it cannot feel it.






The rows of this table do not agree, and the reason says something about what this circuit does. Living among their own kind, the animals with drives do better than the control. Sharing a world with control animals, they do not: there it is the control animals that gain.
The animals with drives do not get more food. They eat less than the control and move less. What they gain is that a warm body burns its food more slowly. A fed animal resting in a warm place leaves the bushes around it to whoever is still walking, and in a shared world that is the control animals. Food is scarce enough for this to matter: either population, alone in a world with half as many animals, does far better than at full numbers.
So the head-to-head row here measures who wins the race for berries, and resting is a poor way to win a race. It does not show that resting is a mistake for the animal that does it. Inside the populations that have the circuit, where every animal competes with others that also rest, evolution left the strength of rest where it was designed and made the hunger gate stronger.


Is the circuit used?



Silencing hungry does not make the animal less hungry. It removes the one signal that tells the warmth cells to stand down, so the animal rests where it is warm while its stomach empties. That is why this lesion costs the most: of the four cells, hungry is the one that decides.
cold and warm_seek form one chain, so silencing either gives the same result.


How a life is spent



The animals of this stage move less than their control. That is rest at work: a fed animal in a warm place stays there.

title: Affect: states that last
text:
The world: every kind of bush in its own patches
Everything this brain does so far, it does about the present. A bush is in front of it, so it bites. The skin is cold, so it walks. The stomach is empty, so it forages. When the cause is gone, the behaviour is gone in the same moment.
But some events say something about the minutes that follow. An animal that has just eaten well is probably standing in a good place. An animal that has just been hurt is probably standing in a bad one. To use that, the brain has to keep something of the event after it is over. This stage adds two such states.
In the world of the previous stage the bushes of every kind were spread evenly. There, a meal says nothing about the place: the bush that was just emptied stays empty for a long time, and what grows next to it is as likely to be poison as anywhere else. A state that lasts has nothing to work with.
So the bushes now grow in patches, and every patch holds one kind. After a good meal, the neighbouring bushes are most likely good as well. After a poison bite, the neighbours are most likely poison too. What just happened says what is near.
The rest is as before: the world is cold, the hot springs are spread evenly, and the four kinds of berry bush are new in every life, half of them poison.

title: Affect: states that last
text:
The biology: affect
A drive, as in the previous stage, follows the body: the hunger cell fires for as long as the stomach is empty and stops when it is full. An affective state is different in one respect. Something sets it off, and then it stays for a while by itself, after its cause has gone.
In small animals such states are carried by neuromodulators: substances that a few cells release and that reach many cells at once. They are released quickly and cleared slowly, and that slowness is the memory. The roundworm C. elegans slows down and stays where it is for minutes after it has found food, under the influence of serotonin. After a harmful touch it speeds away, and keeps going well after the touch has ended.
Such a state has two sides. It is good or bad, and it makes the animal more active or less. An animal that is alarmed is in a bad and active state. An animal that is content is in a good and quiet one.

title: Affect: states that last
text:
The circuit
Two modulators, each released by one event and cleared slowly, and three new cells.

Alarm. Pain releases the modulator alarm. It drives a new cell, flee, which pushes the animal forward. After a poison bite the animal keeps going for a short while, out of the patch of poison.
Serotonin. A new cell, fed, fires when the animal tastes food, and releases the modulator serotonin. It drives a new cell, settle, which switches on rest, the cell of the previous stage that holds the forward step back. After a meal the animal stays where it ate, also where it is cold.

hungry still shuts rest, as before. So a fed animal stays in the good patch until it is hungry again, and then it forages, with good bushes close by.
The two states are not a second system next to the drives. They act on the same cells: the drives decide what the animal does from what the body needs now, and the two modulators push those same modes for a while after an event.
The wiring is designed. Evolution may tune every strength, and also how fast each modulator is cleared, which sets how long each state lasts.

title: Affect: states that last
text:
Results

Main against control
The control is the brain of the previous stage in this world of patches. It feels pain and tastes food as before, but nothing of either stays with it.






The animals with the two states do better than the control in every seed, and by about the same amount in each. Unlike in the previous stage, the rows of the table agree. Sharing a world with control animals, the animals of this stage also come out ahead: staying in a good patch keeps an animal next to its next meal, and that helps in a race for berries as much as it does among its own kind.
Both populations were still improving when the runs ended. The control improves too: without any lasting state, evolution makes it rest more, which keeps some of the animals near where they ate.


Is the circuit used?



Both new states are used. Silencing fed or settle gives nearly the same result, because they form one chain: without either, a meal leaves no serotonin behind and the animal no longer stays. Silencing flee costs less. The alarm is short and acts only after a poison bite, which is a small part of a life.
Two things from earlier stages have lost their use in this world.

Silencing cold or warm_seek no longer costs anything. In the previous stage a fed animal walked while it was cold, until it found warmth. Here that walk takes it out of a good patch, and staying where the food is turns out to be worth more than being warm.
Switching the learning off costs little. In a patch of one kind, the first bite tells the animal what it needs to know about all the bushes around it, and the alarm carries it away from them. Knowing a poison by its look matters less when poison no longer stands between the good bushes.

Neither was removed. The cells are part of the previous stages as they were frozen, and a later world may need them again.


After a bite



The two states can be seen in what the animals do in the twenty ticks after a bite. After a poison bite the animals of this stage take more steps than the control. After a good meal they take almost none.


How a life is spent



Both populations stand still for most of their life. Much of that time they bite at nothing: an animal that is held in place by rest still has its grasp programme, and a bite costs little.

title: Camera eyes
text:
The world of this chapter
Chapter 1 ended with an animal that steers, avoids what hurts, learns which food to distrust, looks after two needs and carries a mood for a while. It did all of that with five coarse eyes. This chapter builds the brain of an early fish on top of it, and a fish sees far better than a worm. So the first step of the chapter is not a new part of the brain. It is better eyes, and a world to use them in.
The last stage of chapter 1 grew every kind of bush in its own patches. That gave the two lasting states their job, and it took the job away from learning: in a patch of one kind, the first bite says everything about the neighbours. The stages of this chapter are about learning, so they need a world in which learning pays.
Several worlds were tried with the animals of chapter 1. Patches that were mostly one kind, with some poison standing between the good bushes, did not bring learning back, however the kinds were mixed. Only a world without patches did, where good and poison bushes stand side by side everywhere. That is the world of this chapter. It is the cold world of the drives stage, with more bushes and more room.
The price is that the two lasting states of the previous stage have less to do here. That is accepted. Not every part of a brain matters equally in every place.
The food is as before: four kinds of berry bush, new in every life, half of them poison.

title: Camera eyes
section: The biology: an eye that forms an image
text:
The biology: an eye that forms an image
The eyes of early bilaterians were little more than light-sensitive spots that told bright from dark and one side from the other. Vertebrates have camera eyes: a lens throws an image onto a sheet of receptors, and the brain receives many small views side by side. With the image came a part of the midbrain that holds a map of it, the optic tectum. In a fish or a frog the tectum picks out something small and moving, turns the eyes and body to it, and starts the escape from something large that grows quickly.
This stage gives the animal the sharper eyes and leaves the tectum out. In this world nothing moves and nothing hunts, so the quick, inborn reactions that the tectum is known for have nothing to react to. A first design, a map that picked the nearest thing in view and steered to it, was tried before any evolution and did not help: the animal already steers to bushes with the reflexes it evolved in chapter 1, and “the nearest thing” is as often an empty bush or a poison one. The other thing a tectum does, letting what the animal has learned choose where to turn, needs the parts of the brain that this chapter adds later.

title: Camera eyes
text:
The change
The animal now looks in nine directions where it had five, and sees one step further.
No cells are added. Every part of the brain that listened to the five old eyes now listens to all nine, and every connection from every eye is its own: there is no copy of a circuit per eye, and nothing forces two eyes to mean the same. What a look is worth, and in which direction it counts, is for evolution and for the animal’s own learning to settle, eye by eye.
The four new eyes sit between the old ones. They do not start silent. Each new connection starts as the average of the same connection from the two neighbouring eyes, so that the animal makes sense of what the new eyes see from its first tick. Nine eyes send nearly twice as much as five, which would overwhelm the cells that listen, so all connections from the eyes are made weaker by the same factor.

title: Camera eyes
text:
Results

The run
This stage has no control. Its question is not whether a new circuit earns its place, but whether the animals of chapter 1 settle into the new world with their new eyes. The comparison is with the population they started from.






The curve of a run is hard to read here, because every generation lives in a new world and the worlds differ a great deal. The fair comparison puts the starting population and the evolved one in the same worlds. That is the table below, in the row for this stage’s world: the evolved animals do clearly better than the ones they descend from.





Room
The same table shows why the world was made larger. With the same animals and the same density of bushes, both populations do better when there is more room, and the better population gains the most.
The reason is in what is left standing. A good bush is emptied in a few bites. A poison bush loses one berry and keeps the rest. Where many animals forage close together, the bushes that still carry berries are more and more the poison ones, and the good ones run out nearby although the world as a whole grows plenty. A population that forages better does this to itself faster. In a small world that hides part of an improvement, so the world of this chapter has twice the area of the worlds of chapter 1.


Is learning used again?



Yes, and more than at any point in chapter 1. With learning switched off, the animals lose about half of their fitness and eat far more poison. In the patches of the previous stage the same switch cost nothing.
The new eyes have a part in that. The lesson of a poison bite is written into the connections from every eye, so nine eyes carry it where five did, and the animal recognises the poison from more directions.
The two lasting states of the previous stage, flee and the chain from fed to settle, matter little in this world, as expected without patches. They stay in the brain.
When the four new eyes started silent instead, the animals did worse after the same number of generations, and the new eyes were still weak at the end. Evolution alone needs a long time to give dozens of new connections per cell a meaning; copying the neighbours gives it something to adjust.


How a life is spent



These animals find food almost at once, and most of them still die young. What kills them is not hunger but poison: an animal bites the same kinds of poison bush again and again, far more often than it would need to find out which ones they are, and a few bites cost as much as the stomach it was born with. When it does eat well, it keeps biting on a full stomach, which gains nothing and strips the good bushes around it.
Both are failures of learning, and they set the task for the stages that follow: to tell apart things that look alike, to remember what was learned about each, and to learn what is worth wanting and not only what to avoid.
